title: Do activation-based jailbreak probes detect harmful intent before or after the harmful tokens are generated?

original_idea.problem: Whether the activation signal for jailbreak detection is present at the prompt stage or only emerges during generation is not systematically studied.
original_idea.direction: Extract activations at prompt-final token, after 5 generated tokens, and after 20 tokens. Train separate probes at each point. Compare AUROC.
original_idea.why_it_matters: Determines whether pre-generation filtering is sufficient or output monitoring is always required.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: detection timing -> determines whether pre-generation filtering works -> directly affects deployment architecture for safety monitoring. Addresses a practical question with clear implications.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires activation extraction at multiple generation stages and training linear probes. Intermediate ML skills needed. Activation hooks and generation-time extraction add complexity for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Focused first deliverable: an AUROC comparison across 3 extraction points. Clear methodology. Few dependencies beyond a model and a jailbreak dataset.

novelty.reasoning: The question of when jailbreak signals become detectable is partially addressed. 'LLM Jailbreak Detection for (Almost) Free!' (EMNLP 2025 Findings) trains probes on intermediate representations at the prompt stage. JBShield (USENIX Security 2025) uses representation-based detection. However, the specific systematic comparison of AUROC at prompt-final-token vs. after 5 generated tokens vs. after 20 generated tokens has not been directly published. Most existing work focuses on prompt-stage detection or output filtering separately, without a controlled timing comparison. The idea of extracting activations at multiple generation stages and training separate probes at each point adds a novel experimental contribution.
